title: Of Studies
author: Francis Bacon
summary: Studies serve three ends: delight (in private and in retirement), ornament (in conversation) and ability (in judging and managing business). Learned men handle affairs better than merely experienced ones.

Too much time in study is sloth; using learning too much for show is affectation; judging only by its rules is a scholar's whim. Studies perfect nature and are perfected by experience: natural abilities are like natural plants that need pruning by study.

Crafty men condemn studies, simple men admire them, and wise men use them. Read not to contradict and confute, nor to believe and take for granted, nor to find talk and discourse, but to weigh and consider.

Some books are to be tasted, others swallowed, and some few chewed and digested — read only in parts, read but not curiously, or read wholly with diligence and attention. 'Distilled books' (summaries) are like distilled water — flashy things.

Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; writing an exact man. One who writes little needs a great memory; one who confers little needs a present wit; one who reads little needs much cunning to seem to know what he does not.

Histories make men wise; poets witty; mathematics subtle; natural philosophy deep; moral philosophy grave; logic and rhetoric able to contend. 'Abeunt studia in mores' — studies pass into character. Every defect of the mind can be cured by a fit study, as bodily diseases by exercises: bowling for the stone and kidneys, shooting for the lungs, walking for the stomach, riding for the head. A wandering wit should study mathematics; one who cannot distinguish should study the schoolmen ('cymini sectores' — splitters of hairs); one who cannot argue should study lawyers' cases.

Francis Bacon (1561–1626), lawyer and scientist, is regarded as the first major English essayist and the father of the scientific (empirical) method. 'Of Studies' was the first essay in his collection of ten essays (1597), revised in 1612.
Style: aphoristic — short, pithy, balanced sentences full of practical wisdom; simile ('natural abilities are like natural plants').

Present continuous for actions happening now or planned (I am watching …); simple future with will/shall. Noun ↔ adjective (intelligence — intelligent, courage — courageous). Summary writing: notes first, then the main points in a short paragraph without examples.

sa2: What broader lesson does Bacon's essay convey about the role of studies?
Studies shape our character and cure the defects of the mind, just as exercise cures the body. Used in the right measure and checked by experience, they make us wise, able and balanced.
What are the three uses of studies?
Studies serve for delight in private and in retirement, for ornament in conversation, and for ability in judging and managing business.
Why does Bacon compare natural abilities to natural plants?
Just as plants need pruning to grow well, our natural talents need to be trimmed and shaped by study. Study improves raw abilities, and experience in turn corrects study.
How should we read, according to Bacon?
Not to contradict others, nor to believe everything blindly, nor merely to find things to talk about, but to weigh and consider what we read.
Explain: 'Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested.'
Some books need to be read only in parts, some read quickly without close attention, and a few important ones read fully, carefully and thoughtfully so that we absorb them.
How do reading, conference and writing help a man?

Reading fills the mind with knowledge, conference (discussion) makes one quick and ready in reply, and writing makes one exact and precise. Without them one needs a great memory, a present wit or cunning.
sa3: How can different defects of the mind be cured by studies, according to Bacon?

Bacon says every impediment of the mind can be removed by a fitting study, as exercises cure bodily ills. A wandering mind should study mathematics, one who cannot distinguish should study the schoolmen, and one who cannot argue should study lawyers' cases.
Comment on Bacon's style in 'Of Studies'.

His style is aphoristic: short, balanced, pithy sentences that pack much wisdom into few words, such as 'Reading maketh a full man'. He uses similes and metaphors (plants, tasting books) and parallel structure, and many lines have become proverbs.

or: What, according to Bacon, are the dangers of excessive study?

Too much study is sloth, making one lazy. Using learning too much for show is affectation, and judging everything only by bookish rules is the whim of a scholar. Study must be balanced and corrected by experience.

sa3: 'Histories make men wise; poets witty …' Explain.

Bacon says each subject develops a quality: history gives wisdom through lessons of the past, poetry wit, mathematics subtlety, natural philosophy depth, moral philosophy seriousness, and logic and rhetoric the power to argue. What we study passes into our character.
